pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Static electricity and sparks

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum):** KS3 'Electricity and electromagnetism / Static electricity' — statutory wording 'separation of positive or negative charges when objects are rubbed together: transfer of electrons, forces between charged objects' and 'the idea of electric field, forces acting across the space between objects not in contact' (verified by fetch).

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** National (NGSS): MS-PS2-3 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-3]' (DCI PS2.B: electric forces can be attractive or repulsive and depend on the charges and the distance) and MS-PS2-5 'Conduct an investigation... [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-5]', whose clarification names electrically-charged tape and pith balls and permits first-hand experiences OR simulations, with assessment limited to qualitative evidence (verified by fetch).

- **Operational details:** Static electricity is the child's first encounter with charge as something that can be SEPARATED and held still, rather than flowing in a circuit. The core ideas: rubbing two insulators together TRANSFERS ELECTRONS from one to the other (it does not create charge), leaving one object negative (gained electrons) and the other positive (lost electrons); like charges repel and unlike attract, with forces acting ACROSS a gap (a first electric-field idea); and a discharge is electrons jumping back when a path appears — lightning being the giant case. The single most important and most-violated point is conservation: charge is not made by rubbing, only MOVED, and in solids it is always the negative electrons that move (the positive object simply lost some). Teaching is most effective with vivid demonstrations (balloons, rods, charged tape, a Van de Graaff) paired with an electron-transfer model that makes the invisible movement and its conservation explicit, and with the like/unlike rule tested directly on suspended charged objects. This topic has a strong TWO-tier anchor.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional / early-formal, ~11–12).
bestPractices: Lead with conservation: rubbing does not CREATE charge, it MOVES electrons from one material to the other — demonstrate with an electron tally (one object ends negative by gaining the very electrons the other lost).
Insist that in solids only ELECTRONS move: the positively charged object did not gain positive charge, it LOST electrons. This single correction pre-empts most static errors.
Establish the force rule directly and symmetrically: like charges repel, unlike attract — test on two suspended charged rods so repulsion (which needs two like charges) is seen, not just attraction.

Use the field/forces-at-a-distance idea to connect static to magnetism and gravity (already-met non-contact forces): the force acts across the gap, and gets stronger with more charge and smaller distance (the MS-PS2-3 factors).

Address the neutral-object case explicitly: a charged balloon sticks to a NEUTRAL wall by polarising/inducing charge — so attraction alone does not prove the other object is oppositely charged; only repulsion confirms a like charge.

Connect static to current as complementary: static is charge built up with NO path to flow (often on insulators); give it a path and it discharges — the spark/shock — with lightning as the same process at huge scale.

Use safe vivid demos (balloon on hair/wall, polythene and acetate rods, charged sticky tape, Van de Graaff) and have pupils PREDICT attract/repel before testing; NGSS sanctions first-hand experiences or simulations and keeps the evidence qualitative.
keyRepresentations: Electron-transfer before/after diagram — two neutral materials, then rubbing moves electrons across, with a charge tally showing one negative (gained) and one positive (lost), total charge unchanged.
Suspended charged-rods demo — like rods swing apart (repel), unlike swing together (attract), showing forces across a gap.
Balloon-on-wall induction picture — a charged balloon polarising a neutral wall, explaining attraction without opposite net charge.
Electric-field-as-force-across-space sketch — linking static forces to magnetism/gravity as non-contact forces that strengthen with charge and weaken with distance.
Lightning as scaled-up discharge — charge separation in a cloud, then electrons jumping along a path to neutralise, the same process as a doorknob spark.
commonMisconceptions: 'Rubbing creates charge / makes electricity' — charge is conserved; rubbing only TRANSFERS electrons from one object to the other.
'Protons / positive charges move' — in solids only electrons move; the positively charged object did not gain positives, it LOST electrons.
Thinking both rubbed objects get the same sign of charge — they get OPPOSITE charges (one gains the electrons the other loses).
Believing attraction proves the other object is oppositely charged — a charged object also attracts a NEUTRAL one by induction/polarisation; only REPULSION proves two like charges.
Confusing static charge with current — static is charge held still with no flow path (often on insulators); current is charge flowing in a complete circuit.
Thinking charged objects must touch to exert a force — the force acts across a gap (the electric-field idea), strengthening with more charge and smaller separation.
Believing lightning only travels cloud-to-ground — discharge can occur within a cloud, cloud-to-cloud, or ground-to-cloud; it is charge separation neutralising along any available path.
Treating metals as where static builds up — charge accumulates on INSULATORS; on a conductor it would flow away to earth.

learn.summary: Static electricity for ages 11–12: rubbing two insulators together does not create charge, it transfers electrons from one material to the other, leaving one negative (gained electrons) and the other equally positive (lost electrons). Like charges repel and unlike attract, with the force acting across a gap and strengthening with more charge and smaller separation. A charged object also attracts a neutral one by inducing/polarising its charge, so only repulsion proves two like charges. A discharge is electrons jumping along a newly available path — a spark or, at huge scale, lightning. A dynamic model that makes the invisible electron transfer visible, countable and conserved may be combined with direct testing of the force rule on suspended charged objects, kept qualitative to match assessment limits; the sources do not establish that this combination outperforms other media.

activities.title: Counting electrons: rubbing moves charge, it does not make it
feedback: If a learner says the cloth/hair stays neutral or that rubbing 'makes' charge: the tally shows the same electrons that arrived on one object came off the other — count them; none appeared from nowhere.
If a learner says both objects become negative: electrons LEFT one object to reach the other, so the giver must be left positive and the receiver negative — they cannot both gain.
If a learner says positive charges or protons moved: in solids the protons stay put; only electrons move, so a positive object is one missing electrons, not one that gained positives.
activities.rationale: The conservation point is the single most-violated idea in static electricity. A visible, countable before/after electron tally makes the invisible transfer and its conservation explicit, directly confronting 'rubbing creates charge' and 'protons move' errors. A dynamic model can show the hopping and recomputed totals that a fixed diagram cannot animate, though a labelled before/after diagram with a charge tally can still teach the same conservation idea.
sourceClaims: KS3 'Static electricity' statutory wording: separation of positive or negative charges when objects are rubbed together, transfer of electrons, forces between charged objects; and the idea of electric field, forces acting across the space between objects not in contact.

The 'rubbing creates charge', 'positive charges/protons move', 'attraction proves opposite charge', and static-vs-current confusions are documented difficulties best addressed by an electron-transfer model that makes conservation visible, testing repulsion directly, and explaining induction of neutral objects.
learnerActions: Start from two neutral objects shown with equal numbers of positive and negative charges (e.g. a balloon and a head of hair, or a polythene rod and a cloth).
Rub them together and watch individual electrons hop one by one from one material onto the other, with a running tally of each object's charge.
Read the tally after rubbing: confirm the balloon/rod is negative by exactly the number of electrons the hair/cloth lost, which is now equally positive.
State in your own words where the charge came from: nothing was created; electrons were only moved, so the two objects carry equal and opposite charge.
activities.intendedInsight: Charge is conserved: rubbing separates and transfers existing electrons rather than generating new charge, and in solids it is the negative electrons that move, so the positive object is positive precisely because it lost them.

activities.title: Attract or repel? Testing the force rule across a gap
feedback: If a learner predicts two same-rubbed balloons will attract: both carry the same sign, and like charges repel — the committed prediction surfaces a vague 'charge pulls things together' idea before the test corrects it.

If a learner concludes the wall must be oppositely charged because the balloon sticks: the wall is neutral; its charges only rearranged (polarised), so attraction does not prove an opposite net charge — repulsion does.
If a learner thinks objects must touch to feel the force: the balloons repel across a gap, showing a force acting at a distance that weakens as they move apart.
activities.rationale: Testing repulsion directly on suspended objects makes the symmetric like/unlike rule observable rather than inferred only from attraction, and the neutral-wall case separates genuine opposite charge from induced attraction. The predict-then-test structure exposes reasoning before the result. Varying charge and separation addresses the strength factors named in the force standard while keeping the evidence qualitative.
sourceClaims: NGSS MS-PS2-3 asks students to determine factors affecting the strength of electric and magnetic forces (DCI PS2.B: electric forces can be attractive or repulsive and depend on the charges and the distance), and MS-PS2-5 asks for evidence that fields exist between objects not in contact, with its clarification naming electrically-charged tape and pith balls, permitting first-hand experiences or simulations, and limiting assessment to qualitative evidence.

The 'rubbing creates charge', 'positive charges/protons move', 'attraction proves opposite charge', and static-vs-current confusions are documented difficulties best addressed by an electron-transfer model that makes conservation visible, testing repulsion directly, and explaining induction of neutral objects.
learnerActions: Predict, before releasing, whether two objects rubbed the same way (e.g. two balloons rubbed on wool, or two like-charged rods) will swing together or apart, and give a reason.
Suspend the two charged objects on threads and bring them close; observe that they repel and swing apart.
Bring a charged balloon near a NEUTRAL wall and watch it lean in and stick as the wall's charges shuffle (induction/polarisation).
Compare the two outcomes and decide: what does repulsion tell you about the two charges, and why does attraction NOT prove the other object is oppositely charged?
Vary the amount of charge and the separation (e.g. with sliders or by moving objects nearer) and describe qualitatively how the force changes.
activities.intendedInsight: Like charges repel and unlike attract, but attraction alone is ambiguous because a charged object also attracts a neutral one by induction; only repulsion confirms two like charges. The force acts across a gap and strengthens with more charge and smaller distance.

activities.title: From spark to lightning: discharge as charge flowing back
feedback: If a learner says static 'isn't real electricity' and has nothing to do with current: the spark is the built-up charge briefly flowing — static is charge at rest, current is charge in motion, the same charge in both.

If a learner thinks rubbing a metal held in the hand charges it: charge flows straight through a conductor that is connected to earth (for example through your hand), so it does not build up. Charge builds up on insulators, where it cannot move away, or on a conductor that is insulated from earth (like a Van de Graaff dome), until a path appears.
If a learner thinks lightning only goes cloud-to-ground: discharge follows any available path, so it can occur within a cloud, cloud-to-cloud, or ground-to-cloud.
activities.rationale: Connecting static to current as complementary states, and lightning to an everyday spark, builds the required link between discharge and large-scale phenomena while confronting the 'static and current are unrelated' misconception. Keeping the treatment qualitative matches the assessment boundary.
sourceClaims: The 'rubbing creates charge', 'positive charges/protons move', 'attraction proves opposite charge', and static-vs-current confusions are documented difficulties best addressed by an electron-transfer model that makes conservation visible, testing repulsion directly, and explaining induction of neutral objects.
learnerActions: With built-up charge on an object, give the electrons a path (e.g. press a 'discharge' control, or touch a metal handle after rubbing) and observe the spark.
Describe what the spark is: the separated electrons flowing to neutralise the charge difference once a path exists.
Zoom out to a thundercloud and relate cloud charge separation and a lightning strike to the same discharge process at a far larger scale.
Explain how static (charge held still, often on an insulator, with no flow path) and current (charge flowing in a complete circuit) are related — a discharge is a brief flow of the same charge.
Consider that lightning can travel within a cloud, cloud-to-cloud, or ground-to-cloud, not only cloud-to-ground.
activities.intendedInsight: A discharge is separated charge neutralising along any available path; static (charge at rest) and current (charge in motion) are two states of the same charge, and lightning is a city-scale version of a doorknob spark.

activities.title: Check your reasoning: signs, forces and discharge
feedback: For electron direction: electrons move onto the object that ends up negative; the other is left positive by the same amount.
For the attraction item: attraction is consistent with either an opposite charge OR a neutral object polarised by induction, so it is not conclusive — only repulsion is.
For the fill-in: electrons are transferred; the total charge is unchanged.
Reasoning answers (why, explain) show more than a recognised option; ask learners to justify rather than only select.
activities.rationale: A set of well-defined checks lets learners self-test the create-charge, protons-move, attraction-proves-opposite and static-vs-current errors after working with the models. Recognition items confirm the rules but do not by themselves elicit independent construction, so the explain/justify prompts are included to require learner-generated reasoning.
sourceClaims: The 'rubbing creates charge', 'positive charges/protons move', 'attraction proves opposite charge', and static-vs-current confusions are documented difficulties best addressed by an electron-transfer model that makes conservation visible, testing repulsion directly, and explaining induction of neutral objects.
learnerActions: Given two named materials rubbed together, choose which way electrons move and the resulting sign of each object.
Sort pairs of charged objects into those that attract and those that repel.
Answer whether attraction proves the other object is oppositely charged, and explain (no — it could be neutral and attracted by induction).
Complete: 'Rubbing transfers ____; it does not create charge.'
Explain in a sentence or two how a doorknob spark and lightning are the same process.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate the mechanism and rules: direction of electron transfer, resulting opposite charges, like/unlike forces, the ambiguity of attraction, and discharge as flowing charge.

constraints: Keep all reasoning qualitative (relative charge, attract/repel, stronger/weaker): the referenced standards limit assessment to qualitative evidence and do not expect quantitative field or force calculations at this age.
In solids, only electrons move; always describe a positive object as one that LOST electrons, never as one that gained positive charge or protons.

Always pair attraction observations with the induction caveat: attraction can arise from a neutral polarised object, so only repulsion confirms two like charges — do not let learners treat attraction as proof of opposite charge.

Reference/tap-to-reveal scenes (balloon, Van de Graaff, lightning) can teach vocabulary and examples but cannot animate electrons transferring or forces recomputing; use them as a supporting reference layer alongside a model that does show the mechanism.
A tap-to-reveal or selection task checks the rules but does not require learners to construct explanations; include tasks where learners state where charge came from and why in their own words.
First-hand demos (balloon on hair/wall, polythene and acetate rods, charged sticky tape, Van de Graaff) and simulations are both sanctioned; use safe demos and have pupils predict before testing.

An in-role persona (storm scientist or Franklin) can engage learners and probe their ideas Socratically; because a conversation does not itself display the electron transfer or the attract/repel forces, pair it with a model or demo that does, using it as a warm-up or debrief rather than the sole teacher.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source marks the two curriculum-standard claims as verified and the IOP misconceptions claim as unverified (verified:false); treat the misconception-remediation claim as not independently confirmed here.

The original recommendation leaned heavily on a specific interactive sandbox as the 'ideal' medium and asserted 'no static medium can show the transfer'; this has been softened. A labelled before/after diagram with a charge tally can also teach conservation, and the dynamic model is presented as one effective option with a stated affordance, not a necessity, since the sources do not establish comparative efficacy.

The summary's 'strongest learning combines' wording was softened to qualified 'may be combined' because the sources do not establish that a dynamic model plus suspended-rod testing outperforms other media.
The original '3D adds nothing' judgement has been omitted as a catalog preference, not a pedagogical law; a spatial 3D storm scene could add atmosphere without changing the core qualitative insight.
Constraint 7 was revised to drop the comparative 'better shown than discussed' claim and keep only the affordance that a conversation does not itself display the transfer or forces.
Sliders/tally/discharge controls and the suspended-rods and balloon-on-wall setups are preserved as concrete, optional ways to make the mechanism visible, not as mandatory product features.

The KS3 statutory-wording claim is cited only on the conservation/transfer activity it directly supports and was kept off the discharge/lightning activity because it does not mention discharge, current, or lightning; only the IOP static-vs-current claim directly supports that activity's principle.

assess.poeTask: Rub two inflated balloons on wool and hang them close together on threads. Before letting go, ask the child to predict whether they will swing together or apart, and why. Many predict they attract ('both are charged, charge is sticky'); they in fact repel because the charges are alike. The committed pre-observation reason reveals whether the child holds like-repels or a vague 'charge pulls things together' idea.
probeDeeper: The charged rod picks up tiny bits of paper that aren't charged at all. How can a charged object attract a neutral one?
Why do you get a small shock and a spark when you touch a metal door handle after walking across a carpet? Where does the charge go?
Two balloons both rubbed on hair push apart when brought close. What must be true about their charges — and what would it mean if they pulled together?
If rubbing created charge rather than moving it, the cloth would gain nothing. How could we check whether the cloth is charged too?
assess.correctAnswer: The cloth becomes positively charged. Rubbing did not make any new charge — it transferred electrons from the cloth onto the rod. The rod gained electrons (negative), so the cloth is left with an equal and opposite positive charge. Charge is separated and moved, not created.

errorPatterns.pattern: Charge created by friction: 'rubbing makes electricity/charge; the cloth stays neutral because the rod just made its own charge'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish conservation of charge: rubbing only separates existing charge. Test the cloth against a known charge to show it is oppositely charged.
errorPatterns.distractor: The cloth stays neutral — rubbing simply creates a charge on the rod.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Tier-2 answer says the cloth is unchanged/neutral, or that rubbing 'generates' charge rather than moving it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Both objects gain the same charge: 'the cloth also becomes negative, the same as the rod'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Electrons LEFT the cloth to reach the rod, so the two must be opposite; use the transfer picture (one gains, the other loses).
errorPatterns.distractor: The cloth also becomes negatively charged, the same as the rod.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Tier-1 answer gives both objects the same sign of charge.

errorPatterns.pattern: Static and current electricity are unrelated 'stuffs': 'static isn't real electricity — it has nothing to do with current or circuits'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show discharge (spark/lightning) is a brief flow of the same charge — static is charge at rest, current is charge in motion.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When linking discharge/lightning to circuits, denies any connection between built-up charge and flowing charge.

errorPatterns.pattern: Charge/magnetism conflation: 'the charged rod is magnetic, that's why bits of paper jump to it'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast: magnets attract iron only; a charged rod attracts light neutral objects of any material by induction — different phenomenon.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains attraction using magnet language, or expects only metals/iron to be attracted.

responseLevels.gap: Says rubbing creates or makes charge/electricity; thinks only the rod is charged, or explains attraction as magnetism.
responseLevels.full: Explains that rubbing separates charge by transferring electrons (rod negative, cloth equally positive — nothing created), uses attract/repel to reason about unseen charges, and connects everyday discharge and lightning as the same charge flowing back — coordinating the ideas and transferring to a new case.
responseLevels.partial: States that electrons are transferred and that like charges repel while unlike attract, and links lightning to a spark, but treats these as separate facts — cannot say the cloth must be equally and oppositely charged, or why a charged rod attracts neutral paper.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You rub a plastic rod with a cloth and the rod becomes negatively charged. What happens to the cloth — is it charged now, and if so how is it charged? Explain where the rod's extra charge came from.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 'rubbing creates charge' idea predicts the cloth stays neutral (the rod just 'made' its own charge) or becomes negative like the rod. The electron-transfer model requires the cloth to be equally and oppositely charged. It is hard to say 'the cloth is positive, by the same amount, because electrons left it' without holding the transfer model, and the create-charge child cannot get there.
